FermiWick

Fermion operators, as symbols and as matrices

Wick's theorem, mean field, Gutzwiller projectors and exact diagonalisation for fermions, in the Wolfram Language

InstallShowcase PDF Manual PDFGitHub
  • Version 0.2.0 (2026-11-10)
  • Mathematica 13.0 or later
  • 85 tests pass
  • GPL-3.0-or-later

What it does

FermiWick does by computer the algebra one does on paper with fermion ladder operators, in the order of a calculation.

  • OperatorsIt brings products to normal order site by site, keeping the local operators — densities, spins, double occupancy, doublons, projectors — compact. It decomposes products of ladder operators into these local operators and recognizes the operators that act on several sites: , the scalar chirality and operators of your own.
  • ContractionsIt evaluates expectation values by Wick's theorem in a Gaussian state that you declare by its symmetries — spin rotations, rotations about z, charge, time reversal — or by rules for its contractions, with normal and anomalous contractions; ContractionTable shows which contractions survive.
  • Mean fieldIt gives the Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov Hamiltonian of an operator of any order, with its constant.
  • Gutzwiller projectorsIt handles projected operators and their expectation values in the Gutzwiller approximation.
  • MatricesIt writes any operator as a sparse matrix on the Fock space of a few sites, or on a sector of fixed particle number and spin, and finds ground states, expectation values and Green's functions: a small cluster is solved exactly, and a symbolic result checked.
  • LaTeXIt writes any result in LaTeX, and writes Wick's theorem out with the contractions drawn.

Sites and spins are symbols, so the same calculation holds on any lattice and for any filling; with numbers for the sites, the same expressions become matrices.

Scope. FermiWick computes exact symbolic expressions for spin-½ fermions, and their matrices on clusters of up to about a million states. Bosons and other flavours are outside its scope, and so are the lattice symmetries (momentum, point group) that dedicated codes use to diagonalise larger clusters.

A first example

Operators. The commutator of two exchange terms that share a site, written back in spin operators, is the scalar chirality; and the spin of a site is only when the site is singly occupied:

Needs["FermiWick`"]

ToSpinChargeBasis[OperatorCommutator[SdotS[1, 2], SdotS[2, 3]]]
ToSpinChargeBasis[SdotS[1, 1]]

Contractions. A state invariant under spin rotations, with hopping and singlet pairing on every bond; in the exchange, hopping and pairing enter with the same weight:

state = SpinSingletState["Pairing" -> Δ];
WickVEV[SdotS[1, 2], state]

Mean field. The mean-field Hamiltonian of has a hopping field, a pairing field and a constant, the coefficients of , of and of :

mf = MeanField[J SdotS[1, 2], state];
fields = OperatorCoefficients[mf];
{fields[cDag[1, "↑"] ** c[2, "↑"]], fields[cDag[1, "↑"] ** cDag[2, "↓"]], fields[1]}

The same works at any order. For the six-fermion chirality each bond receives a hopping from the path through the third site:

mfc = OperatorCoefficients[MeanField[-Jc SdotScrossS[1, 2, 3], state]];
{mfc[cDag[1, "↑"] ** c[2, "↑"]], mfc[cDag[1, "↑"] ** cDag[2, "↓"]]}

Matrices. The same operators on the two-site sector with two electrons and : the spectrum of the Hubbard dimer, exact in and :

Needs["FermiWick`Fock`"]
hop = Sum[cDag[1, s] ** c[2, s] + cDag[2, s] ** c[1, s], {s, $Spins}];
sector = FockSector[FockSpace[{1, 2}], "N" -> 2, "Sz" -> 0];
Eigenvalues[Normal[FockMatrix[-t hop + U (DOp[1] + DOp[2]), sector]]]

LaTeX. WickTeX writes the expansion with the contractions drawn (LaTeX package simpler-wick):

WickTeX[cDag[1, SpinUp] ** cDag[2, SpinDown] ** c[3, SpinDown] ** c[4, SpinUp], state]

Next. The showcase goes through everything the package does, in this order: local operators and their algebra, the spin–charge basis and the recognition of spin operators, operators of your own, states declared by rules, magnetic and general states, the selection of contractions, the mean field of the Hubbard interaction and of spin models, Gutzwiller projectors with the Brinkman–Rice transition and the enhancement of the exchange, and the matrices of the operators: Hubbard clusters solved exactly, and Wick's theorem checked on them. The manual describes every function. In a notebook, ?FermiWick`* lists the functions and ?Name explains each one.

Installation

Install the paclet of the latest release once:

PacletInstall["https://github.com/n4sd4q/FermiWick/releases/download/v0.2.0/FermiWick-0.2.0.paclet"]

and load it in every session:

Needs["FermiWick`"]
Needs["FermiWick`Gutzwiller`"]   (* Gutzwiller projectors, when needed *)
Needs["FermiWick`Fock`"]         (* matrices and exact diagonalisation, when needed *)

There are no dependencies; the package needs Mathematica 13.0 or later and is tested with 15.0. The quickest start is the guided tour, a notebook to run cell by cell, which comes with the paclet:

NotebookOpen[PacletObject["FermiWick"]["AssetLocation", "Examples"]]

(its source is Examples.wl, which also runs as a script). ?FermiWick`* lists the functions and ?Name explains each one. To use a clone of the repository instead, without installing, PacletDirectoryLoad["/path/to/FermiWick/FermiWick"] before Needs.

Writing operators. c[i, s] and cDag[i, s], with s = SpinUp, SpinDown (or "↑", "↓", or a symbol) — or any labels, c[i], c[i, orbital, s], c[k], with DeclareModeLabels saying what they are; ** multiplies in the given order. The spin sum is Sum[..., {s, $Spins}]:

hopping = Sum[cDag[1, s] ** c[2, s] + cDag[2, s] ** c[1, s], {s, $Spins}];

Checks

The test suite (math -script Tests/RunTests.wls, 85 tests) checks the algebra, the mean-field formulas of the two- and three-spin terms and of the Hubbard interaction, and the states. It checks the symbolic engine against the matrices: the matrix of an expression equals that of its normal order and of its spin–charge form; WickVEV and MeanField give the exact values in random Gibbs states of quadratic Hamiltonians with pairing, on three sites and with two orbitals per site, and in the free ground state of a ring; the symmetries of the states hold on exact Gibbs states of symmetric Hamiltonians. The matrices themselves are checked against the Jordan–Wigner construction, and exact diagonalisation on the Hubbard dimer, a magnetic plaquette and Hubbard rings. sh Development/check_docs.sh checks the documents: every example of the showcase and of the manual is run again in a fresh kernel and must give the output printed, the guided tour must run without messages, and the code of the README must give the formulas shown after it.

Related software

SNEG (Žitko, Comput. Phys. Commun. 182, 2259 (2011)) is the closest relative: a Mathematica package for second quantization, with normal ordering, vacuum expectation values in the empty state or the Fermi sea, composite spin and charge operators, and much more: bosons, Majorana fermions, arbitrary spin and exact diagonalization. Its Wick contractions pair a creator with an annihilator. QuantumAlgebra.jl (Julia) handles bosons and fermions, equations of motion and cumulant expansions. wick&d, SeQuant, pdaggerq, drudge and SymPy's secondquant are built for quantum chemistry: index and tensor algebra and the generation of coupled-cluster equations.

FermiWick adds four things to these:

  • Wick's theorem in a Gaussian state that you declare, with normal and anomalous contractions and a selection of them;
  • the symbolic mean-field Hamiltonian of an operator of any order;
  • Gutzwiller-projected expectation values;
  • the same operators as matrices on symmetry sectors, so that every symbolic result can be checked exactly on a cluster.

It keeps local operators compact and recognizes multi-site ones in the results.
